definition: Identity diffusion names the collapse or fragmentation of a stable, continuous self — the condition in which a person can no longer say with confidence who they are, what is real about their past, or where the boundary between self and world lies. In PKD's work it appears both as a clinical-sounding disorder and as a metaphysical predicament: the protagonist discovers that the identity he took as bedrock was constructed, imposed, or false.
pkd_relevance: The dissolving self is PKD's most persistent character mechanism. He repeatedly builds novels around a man whose name, memories, job, and world turn out to be manufactured, then tracks what remains when those supports are pulled away. This recurs so often that it functions less as a plot device than as PKD's basic intuition about persons: identity is provisional, assembled from unreliable materials, and can be revoked without warning.
in_the_fiction: Ragle Gumm in Time Out of Joint lives inside a fabricated 1959 town built to exploit his talent, his whole civilian identity a stage set. Jason Taverner in Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said wakes to find every record of his existence erased and must reconstruct who he is from nothing. Barney Mayerson, Joe Chip, and many others suffer versions of the same erosion, and androids like Rachael Rosen raise the question from the other side — a manufactured identity that believes itself human.
in_the_exegesis: The Exegesis treats identity diffusion mostly through PKD's own case rather than as an abstract topic. He returns compulsively to the possibility that his empirical self was not the real agent — positing a 'Thomas' personality, a dissociated right-hemisphere self, or an occluded true identity recovered through anamnesis. The unstable 'I' of the fiction thus becomes, in the Exegesis, a first-person problem PKD is trying to solve about himself.
intellectual_background: The phrase 'identity diffusion' comes from Erik Erikson's account of adolescent identity formation and its failures, and the broader theme draws on existentialist worries about authenticity and bad faith, on Jung's individuation, and on mid-century clinical writing about dissociation and depersonalization. PKD read widely and unsystematically in psychology, and the motif also owes much to his lived experience of amphetamine use, multiple marriages, and periods of acute instability.
scholarly_debate: Critics disagree on whether PKD's dissolving selves are primarily a symptom or a philosophy. Biographical readers (Sutin, Arnold) connect them to PKD's documented instability and his lost twin; others read them as a deliberate literary phenomenology of the postmodern self, anticipating later theory about the decentered subject. A further debate concerns whether PKD offers any ground beneath the diffusion — an authentic self that survives — or whether, as some argue, the diffusion goes all the way down.
